Strong options keep a simple star schema for analysis; weaker ones split dimensions into chains of tables that slow every query.
focus: A star schema joins one fact table directly to flat dimension tables; a snowflake splits dimensions into more tables.
Facts hold measures and keys; dimensions hold the descriptive attributes users filter and group by.
Materialized views and metric views give consistent measures across dashboards.

DBX-DAA|D9.how: Security questions describe an analyst or partner who needs access to a function, table or share, and ask for the smallest grant. Unity Catalog's privilege chain usually decides. Strong options grant the needed privilege at the right level, or share data instead of copying it; weaker ones transfer ownership or open whole catalogs.
focus: Using a function or table needs USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA plus EXECUTE or SELECT on the object itself.
Delta Sharing gives another Databricks account read-only access across regions and clouds without copying data.
Owners can grant; prefer a group as owner so access does not depend on one person.

DBX-MLA|D1.how: Platform questions ask which Databricks tool fits a step of the ML workflow: AutoML, Feature Store in Unity Catalog, MLflow tracking, the model registry or the ML runtime. The deciding detail is usually what the tool actually stores or speeds up. Strong options match the tool to its real job; weaker ones assume a feature, such as Photon or online sync, works where it does not.
focus: MLflow keeps a parameter once per run and a metric as a series over steps; runs, artifacts and models are separate things.
Feature tables in Unity Catalog need a primary key, and online publishing has its own prerequisites such as change data feed.
Photon speeds up Spark SQL and DataFrame work, not single-node libraries like scikit-learn or XGBoost on pandas.

DBX-MLA|D2.how: Data processing questions give a Spark or pandas DataFrame and ask for the right summary, filter or test. Read the data type and the exact need: exact versus approximate, per group versus overall, continuous versus categorical. Strong options use the API that returns exactly that; weaker ones compute something close but not equal.
focus: Group-wise statistics come from groupBy with agg, returned as one DataFrame.
Approximate quantiles are fast; an exact median needs a relative error of 0 or an exact function.
Choose the statistical test by the feature types: a t-test compares two group means, chi-square compares two categorical features.

DBX-MLA|D3.how: Model development questions cover training, tuning and evaluation with Spark ML, Optuna or Hyperopt, and plain scikit-learn. Count carefully and look for leakage: many wrong answers come from evaluating on data the model has already seen. Strong options keep the validation set clean and the metric in the units the business uses.
focus: Split before you balance or transform, or duplicated rows leak into validation and inflate the score.
A grid of m by n values with TrainValidationSplit fits m times n models plus one final refit; cross-validation multiplies by the folds.
Load large data once outside the trial function; each distributed trial should get small inputs.

DBX-MLA|D4.how: Deployment questions ask how predictions reach users: batch scoring, streaming or a Model Serving endpoint, and how versions move between them. The deciding detail is when the prediction is needed and who reads it. Strong options pick the simplest mode that meets the timing and refer to models by alias; weaker ones add a real-time endpoint nobody needs.
focus: Nightly scores read the next morning are a batch job writing to a Delta table, not a serving endpoint.
Load a model by its Unity Catalog alias (for example @Champion) so jobs follow promotions without edits.
Serving endpoints split traffic between served models; a configuration update keeps the old version serving until the new one is ready.

DBX-ASD|D1.how: Architecture questions ask what Spark does when code runs: which jobs, stages and tasks appear, where memory goes, and what a session shares. Read the code for actions, shuffles and caching. Strong options follow Spark's execution model step by step; weaker ones assume work is reused or shared when it is not.
focus: Transformations are lazy; each action starts a job, and a shuffle splits a job into stages.
Without cache(), a second action recomputes its lineage, though shuffle files can let the UI skip stages.
Temporary views belong to one SparkSession; global temp views live in global_temp and are shared across sessions.

DBX-ASD|D2.how: Spark SQL questions give a query or a read/write call and ask what it returns or why it fails. Check the save mode, the data source options and how the schema is inferred. Strong options name the exact option or clause that produces the result; weaker ones rely on defaults that behave differently.
focus: Save modes differ on retry: append writes the rows again, overwrite replaces, ignore and errorifexists check first.
Plain Parquet overwrite is not atomic; a failed job can leave the path empty or partial, while Delta keeps the old version.
Reading files with SQL needs options such as header for CSV, otherwise columns are named _c0, _c1 and so on.

DBX-ASD|D3.how: DataFrame API questions show a few lines of PySpark and ask for the result or the right method. Trace the rows through joins, groupings and nulls by hand. Strong options get the row count and join semantics exactly right; weaker ones treat NULL keys as equal or forget that a grouped count is a DataFrame.
focus: NULL never matches NULL in a join condition, so left_anti keeps rows with a NULL key.
groupBy().count() returns a DataFrame; count() on it is an action that returns a number.
sortWithinPartitions orders each output file without the shuffle of a global orderBy.

DBX-ASD|D4.how: Tuning questions describe a slow or failing stage and ask for the fix. Read the Spark UI clues: number of tasks, partition sizes, join strategy and where the error happens. Strong options change the one setting or step that matches the symptom; weaker ones add memory or partitions without addressing the cause.
focus: Adaptive Query Execution coalesces small shuffle partitions and can switch a sort-merge join to a broadcast join at runtime.
coalesce reduces partitions without a shuffle; repartition shuffles to balance or increase them.
Executor OOM in a shuffle stage with huge partitions calls for more shuffle partitions, not a larger driver.

DBX-ASD|D5.how: Structured Streaming questions ask what a query does over time and after failures. The checkpoint, the watermark and the output mode decide most answers. Strong options keep state bounded and recovery exact; weaker ones use batch-only operations or unbounded state.
focus: Exactly-once needs a replayable source, a checkpoint and an idempotent or transactional sink.
Without a watermark, dropDuplicates and aggregations keep state forever and it keeps growing.
Sorting a stream is allowed only after an aggregation in complete output mode.

DBX-ASD|D6.how: Deployment questions ask how a Spark application reaches a cluster: cluster managers, deploy modes and Spark Connect. The deciding detail is where the driver runs and what the client holds. Strong options separate the thin client from the server; weaker ones expect JVM or SparkContext access through Spark Connect.
focus: Spark Connect sends unresolved logical plans over gRPC and streams results back as Arrow batches.
With Spark Connect the server can be upgraded on its own, and APIs that need the driver JVM such as sparkContext are not available.
Spark runs on standalone, YARN and Kubernetes cluster managers.

DBX-ASD|D7.how: Pandas API on Spark questions ask when pandas-style code scales and how pandas UDFs work. Check how data is split between workers and what each function receives. Strong options respect the size and shape rules of each API; weaker ones assume one group or one batch can be any size.
focus: pandas API on Spark keeps the pandas syntax but distributes the data, so one machine's memory is no longer the limit.
Pandas UDFs exchange data with Arrow in batches, which is much faster than a row-at-a-time Python UDF.
A Series to Series UDF must return the same length; applyInPandas loads a whole group into one task's memory.

DBX-MLP|D1.how: Professional model development questions mix Spark ML, distributed training and custom pyfunc models at scale. Read the data shape and where training runs. Strong options use the API that fits the workload, batch or stream, single node or many; weaker ones apply an estimator or library where it cannot run.
focus: Spark ML estimators fit on static DataFrames; a fitted PipelineModel can then score a stream.
String labels need StringIndexer before a classifier, and IndexToString maps predictions back.
Multi-node GPU errors such as NCCL failures usually point to networking or environment, not to the model code.

DBX-MLP|D2.how: MLOps questions cover the path from training to production: MLOps Stacks, Asset Bundles, the Unity Catalog registry and monitoring. The deciding detail is usually which environment holds which permissions and when metrics are compared. Strong options compare models on the same current data and keep production locked down.
focus: Compare champion and challenger on the same fresh evaluation data, not on metrics stored when each was trained.
Asset Bundles define jobs, endpoints and their traffic splits as code per target environment.
Data scientists can analyze production through read-only inference tables and monitoring, without write access.

DBX-MLP|D3.how: Deployment questions focus on Model Serving endpoints: rollouts, traffic splits and checks before going live. Read the traffic volume and what the update changes. Strong options pick a rollout that still gives a meaningful signal and validate the environment first; weaker ones run a canary too small to measure.
focus: A configuration update keeps the old version serving until the new one is ready.
At low traffic a small canary percentage yields too few requests; use a larger share or a shadow test.
Validate a model's environment before serving, for example with mlflow.models.predict in a clean environment.

DBX-GAI|D1.how: Design questions ask which shape of generative AI application fits a requirement: plain prompt, RAG, agent with tools or multi-agent. The deciding detail is how fresh the knowledge must be and who decides the next step. Strong options use the simplest pattern that meets the need.
focus: Knowledge that changes often belongs in retrieval with source citations, not in fine-tuning.
A LangChain output parser turns a chat message into a plain string or structured output.
When the fields to extract change per request, pass them in the prompt instead of fixing a schema.

DBX-GAI|D2.how: Data preparation questions are about chunking, parsing and judging retrieval for RAG. Look at the document structure and the metric asked for. Strong options keep meaning together in a chunk and compute precision and recall from the right counts; weaker ones split by characters regardless of structure.
focus: Precision is relevant retrieved over retrieved; recall is relevant retrieved over all relevant in the index.
Tables and sections should be parsed as units, not cut by a fixed character count.
Overlap or small-to-big retrieval keeps the neighbouring sentences that explain an exception.

DBX-GAI|D3.how: Application development questions trace a RAG chain or agent and ask what to fix. Use the trace: check whether retrieval found the right passages before blaming the model. Strong options fix the stage that failed; weaker ones change the prompt when retrieval brought the wrong text.
focus: Wrong passages for a question are a retrieval problem: chunking, embeddings or filters, not the LLM.
Model cards state languages, context length and license, which decide fit before any test.
Genie Chat mode APIs are asynchronous: poll the message status until the query result is ready.

DBX-GAI|D4.how: Assembling and deploying questions cover logging agents with MLflow, packaging files, authentication and vector search. The deciding detail is what the serving environment can reach. Strong options log everything the model needs as artifacts or resources; weaker ones rely on paths that exist only in development.
focus: Log files a chain reads as model artifacts so the endpoint has them; development volume paths may not be reachable.
Declare resources such as indexes and UC functions when logging, so serving gets automatic short-lived credentials.
A Direct Vector Access index takes writes through the API without a source Delta table.

DBX-GAI|D5.how: Governance questions ask how to keep an assistant safe, compliant and affordable. Read the constraint: latency budget, license end date, data type to mask. Strong options combine fast pattern rules with targeted controls and remove data at the source; weaker ones add heavy checks or leave copies behind.
focus: Fixed patterns like card numbers mask fast with rules; names need an entity model.
Removing licensed content means deleting the rows and syncing the index, not just filtering answers.
Rate limits and input size limits guard an endpoint against cost and abuse.

DBX-GAI|D6.how: Evaluation and monitoring questions ask how to measure an application and watch it in production. Prefer evidence from your own task and traces over public rankings. Strong options use the tracing, judges and limits that match the need; weaker ones choose models or budgets by general benchmarks.
focus: Rank candidate models on an evaluation set from your own use case, not a public leaderboard.
MLflow traces from deployed agents let developers step through individual production requests.
Reviewers in the Review App need workspace access and permission on the experiment holding the traces.

DBX-CEA|D1.how: Foundation questions ask what belongs in an agent's context window and why it fails when overloaded. Look for duplicated, stale or irrelevant tokens in the trace. Strong options give the model less but better context; weaker ones add everything in case it helps.
focus: Inject only the memories and chunks relevant to the current request, not the whole store.
Duplicate chunks from several retrievers waste context; deduplicate before passing them on.
Raw tool output such as web pages can be summarized or kept outside the planning context.

DBX-CEA|D2.how: Instruction design questions improve system prompts and Genie instructions. The deciding detail is whether an instruction is specific enough to test. Strong options state the exact format, scope or default and compare versions on the same evaluation data; weaker ones keep vague wording.
focus: Replace vague rules like "format dates correctly" with an exact format and an example.
Compare prompt versions on the same evaluation set; different data makes the scores incomparable.
Genie instructions should define default time ranges and say what is out of scope.

DBX-CEA|D3.how: Retrieval and Genie questions ask why an agent gets the wrong knowledge and how to fix it at the source. Check what was indexed, what values Genie knows and whether retrieval was used. Strong options fix the corpus, metadata or instructions; weaker ones only tune the model.
focus: Keep scratch or draft folders out of the index so retrieval cites approved sources.
Map business words to coded values, for example "open" to status P, in Genie instructions or synonyms.
Reranking narrows many candidates to the few the model needs.

DBX-CEA|D4.how: Memory questions separate session history from long-term memory and ask how much to recall. Read what must persist across conversations and what must be audited. Strong options store durable facts in long-term memory and recall a few relevant ones; weaker ones inject too many or set thresholds that miss them.
focus: Session history covers one conversation; long-term memory holds facts that matter in later ones.
A full audit trail is a separate log from the memory the agent uses for personalization.
Too many recalled memories confuse the model; too strict a threshold misses useful ones.

DBX-CEA|D5.how: Tool design questions ask how tools and MCP servers shape an agent's context. Look at tool names, descriptions and output size. Strong options give tools distinct purposes and small, relevant outputs; weaker ones return whole records or let similar tools overlap.
focus: Return only the fields the agent needs, with filters or pagination, instead of full records.
Distinct names and descriptions stop an agent from using two tools interchangeably.
Let the agent look up a tool's schema before calling it instead of guessing arguments.

DBX-CEA|D6.how: Compression questions ask what to keep when history is compacted. Constraints, open goals and identifiers must survive; noise can go. Strong options define what compaction must preserve; weaker ones summarize freely and lose rules or ids.
focus: Keep user constraints, such as tables not to touch, verbatim through compaction.
Strip repeated debug metadata from tool results before it fills the history.
Preserve the current plan and next step so the agent continues after compaction.

DBX-CEA|D7.how: Multi-agent questions ask how to split work and pass context between agents. Check what each handoff carries and whether shared rules reach every sub-agent. Strong options pass compact structured results and the user's constraints unchanged; weaker ones paraphrase or send full reasoning.
focus: Sub-agents should return short structured results, not their full reasoning.
Pass the user's constraints verbatim to every sub-agent instead of paraphrasing them.
Give parallel writers shared definitions, such as fiscal or calendar quarters, before they start.

PLTR-AWARE|D1.how: Orientation questions ask what Foundry and AIP are for and where each piece sits: data integration south of the Ontology, applications and AI north of it. The deciding detail is usually which layer owns a job. Strong options put logic and definitions in the Ontology once; weaker ones copy them into every app.
focus: Model a business action once in the Ontology so every app edits data the same governed way.
Shared properties give one definition to a field used by several object types.
Use built-in transforms for routine cleaning before writing a custom function.

PLTR-AWARE|D2.how: Developer questions walk through building one workflow: connecting a source, syncing data, modelling objects and actions, and putting them in a Workshop app. Read what the user sees and why. Strong options follow the documented setup and governance; weaker ones assume a shortcut bypasses permissions.
focus: Two users can see different rows in the same table because permissions and markings apply per user.
Inline edits in Workshop still run through the governed action, with its checks.
Pick the egress policy and output location the documentation recommends for the source and enrollment.

PLTR-AWARE|D3.how: Real-world questions ask how a use case is scoped, delivered and kept running with Foundry and AIP: outcomes first, then the workflow, then the AI. The deciding detail is usually ownership or the order of steps. Strong options start from the outcome and keep humans and permissions in the loop.
focus: Agree the outcome and the decision it changes before choosing applications.
Automations run as an owner; if that account is disabled, they stop.
Have an agent write variables through a tool and check it with evals, not instructions alone.
